implementation_notes: Java's production answer is the decorator stack: Resilience4j wraps the call in CircuitBreaker, Bulkhead, TimeLimiter and Retry and attaches the substitute with withFallback(exceptionTypes, fn), so the degradation policy is composition plus a lambda instead of if-trees. What this replaces is the hand-written mode flag - the decorator owns detection, bounding and the recovery switch, and the fallback function owns the substitute (cached value, reduced DTO, placeholder). Use the classic form (try/catch plus Optional.orElseGet) when the module must stay dependency-free or when the degraded answer has to combine several sources; note the floor, since Resilience4j 2 requires Java 17.
code_sketch:
Supplier<Report> report = Decorators.ofSupplier(() -> backend.report(id))
    .withCircuitBreaker(breaker)
    .withTimeLimiter(timeLimiter, scheduler)
    .withFallback(List.of(CallNotPermittedException.class, TimeoutException.class),
                  t -> { metrics.degraded(t); return Report.cached(id); })
    .decorate();
pitfalls: withFallback swallows the original failure into the substitute: log or meter the throwable inside the fallback or the signal is lost.
The fallback lambda runs on the caller's thread inside the decorator; blocking work there consumes the capacity the Bulkhead and TimeLimiter were protecting.
Returning null from a fallback re-introduces NullPointerException downstream - substitute a Null Object or a real default value.

variants.name: Hand-written try/catch fallback (Java 8 form)
variants.implementation_notes: Before decorators, degradation is written by hand: catch the dependency exception and substitute with Optional.orElseGet(cached) on the synchronous path, or chain CompletableFuture.exceptionally(...) on the asynchronous one. This form needs nothing beyond Java 8 and keeps the policy visible at the call site, at the price of repeating the pattern per call and owning the mode bookkeeping (state, thresholds, metrics) yourself.
pitfalls: Catching a broad Exception (or Throwable) here also degrades on programming errors; enumerate the dependency's exception types.
The hand-written form has no detector of its own: without a shared breaker and metrics the fallback fires per request and hides a full outage.
CompletableFuture.exceptionally runs on the completing thread, so blocking substitutes there can starve the common pool.
